Information and Communication Technologies 5G x 5G wireless internet network is 50 times faster than 4G. x It enables superfast data transfer with minimal delay (a latency as low as 1 millisecond). x The US and South Korea have already rolled out the network on a trial basis. x In May 2018, five Nordic countries—Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Finland and Iceland—announced their plan to create the world’s first interconnected 5G region. x In March 19, Germany began auctions of 5G bandwidth spectrum in Bonn. x India plans to begin trials by 2020. India has not yet allocated spectrum for 5G. 5G will enable PMF IAS – Learn Smart 50 x Development of new services for smart mobility and automated transport, accelerating automation of the whole transport sector from maritime to road to air. x Deeper penetration of artificial intelligence (AI)-based technologies (E.g. Amazon’s Alexa, Google’s Google Home, Apples’ Siri, etc.). x Internet of Things (which includes smart wearables and virtual reality headsets). x Commercial application of driverless autonomous vehicles (they can become usable only if they communi- cate with other vehicles and traffic signals). x Low-latency applications, including industrial robots to remote surgery. x Inter-working of different technologies and networks and machine to machine communications. x Integration of satellites in 5G networks for new applications in domains such as agriculture, emergency re- sponse for communities living in rural areas, etc. Health concerns associated with 5G networks x All artificial electromagnetic radiations are bad because our biological systems are not adapted to it. x 5G will promote cell phone use, and therefore human exposures from phones and base stations. x 5G requires Radio Frequency Electromagnetic Fields (RF-EMF) radiation between 600 MHz and 86 GHz. x Typically, RF radiations are nonionizing and cause only dielectric heating effects (unlike ionising radiations like X-rays and gamma rays). x The higher frequencies will concentrate the radiation in a smaller portion of the human body, and children are particularly vulnerable to its effects. x Higher frequencies of 5G will also penetrate much deeper into the human body because of a phenomenon called beam-forming unique to the technology. x Beam forming brings together electromagnetic signals from multiple antennas to create signals with greater intensity and better reach. x In 2011, WHO’s studies detailed the effects of RF-EMF radiations (from 30 kilohertz to 300 gigahertz) on humans as well as rats and concluded that the radiations are “possibly carcinogenic to humans”. x In 2018, a report published in US found RF-EMF of 900 megahertz, used by 3G and 4G networks, led to incidences of malignant heart schwannomas (cancer that attacks nerve tissues) in male and female rats. x Scientists have so far linked 5G to at least 20 ailments, including heart diseases, type-2 diabetes and mental disturbances such as depression, anxiety and suicidal tendencies. Challenges in commercialization of 5G x Businesses and services exploiting its potential are not fully evolved. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 51 x Greater power in the hands of corporations and governments for surveillance. x Internet governance is not evolving to safeguard security and privacy of data. x RF-EMF generated as a consequence of 5G will have a wide range of health impacts. x Loss of employment opportunities in the manufacturing sector due to automation. x More satellites are required, which means rapidly accumulating space junk/debris. x Some scientists suggest designing networks based on fibre optic cables (2 crore times faster than 5G). Fibre Optics x Fiber optics, or optical fiber, refers to the medium & the technology associated with the transmission of information as light pulses along a glass or plastic strand or fiber. x Fiber optics is used in long-distance & high-performance services such as internet, television & telephones. x Advantages over copper cables: 9 Optic fibres have higher bandwidth & transmit speeds. 9 Optic fibres are not affected by electromagnetic interference (reduces speed of transmission). How Fiber optics works? x Fiber optics transmit data in the form of light particles -or photons - that pulse through a fiber optic cable. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 52 x The glass fiber core & the cladding each have a different refractive index that bends light at an angle. x When light signals are sent through the fiber optic cable, they reflect off the core & cladding in a series of zig-zag bounces, adhering to a process called total internal reflection. x The light signals travel 30% slower than the speed because of the denser glass layers. x To renew, or boost, the signal, fiber optics transmission sometimes requires repeaters at distant intervals. Total Internal Reflection x When light travels from an optically denser medium to a rarer medium at the interface, it is partly reflected back into the same medium & partly refracted to the second medium. x This reflection is called the internal reflection. x In total internal reflection, there is no refraction & the entire incident ray will get reflected. Conditions for Total Internal Reflection: 1. The incident ray must be in optically denser medium. 2. The angle of incidence in the denser medium must be greater than the critical angle for the pair of media in contact. Internet of Things x The Internet of Things, or IoT, is a system of interrelated computing devices, mechanical & digital ma- chines, objects, animals, or people. x They are provided with unique identifiers (UIDs). x They transfer data over a network without requiring human-to-human or human-to-computer interaction. x A thing on the internet of things can be: 1. A person with a heart monitor implant, 2. A farm animal with a biochip transponder, 3. An automobile that has built-in sensors to alert the driver when tire pressure is low or any other natural, 4. A human-made object that can have an Internet Protocol (IP) address & is able to transfer data. x IoT devices share the sensor data they collect by connecting to an IoT gateway where data is either sent to the cloud to be analysed or analysed locally. x IoT can also make use of artificial intelligence (AI) & machine learning to aid in making data collecting pro- cesses easier & more dynamic. Project Loon & Starlink Project Loon x It is a project under a Google subsidiary. x It consists of a network of stratospheric balloons designed to bring Internet connectivity to rural & re- mote communities worldwide. x The project involves helium-filled balloons that remain in the stratosphere & create aerial networks. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 57 Starlink x It is a satellite internet constellation being constructed by SpaceX with the aim to bring internet access to rural & underserved areas around the world. x The constellation will consist of 1600 thousand small satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO). What is Starlink system trying to solve? 1. SpaceX wants to cut that long-distance lag. 2. It wants to provide internet access almost anywhere in the world. x The company plans to do this through an unprecedented network of satellites in LEO. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 58 Major problem with the current systems – high latency over long distances x Optic fibre cables have a speed limit — light signals travel 30% slower because of the denser glass layers. x This is not an issue for normal browsing. But over international distances, it leads to high latency, or lag. x The time delay is especially pronounced in long-distance videoconferencing & calls. x Latency also matters to financial institutions. x With markets that move billions in fractions of a second, any delay can lead to big losses over a competitor. x Data beamed over current satellites also has high latency (~0.5 seconds!). x That is because nearly all those spacecraft orbit Earth from about 35,786 kilometres high (GSO). Concerns with Starlink like projects x With so many new satellites in orbit, spaceflight experts are concerned about the potential for creating space junk that can damage or maim other spacecraft. Starlink cannot be better & cannot compete in price with optic fibre x Over short distances fibre-optic will always win as it can carry much more data at low cost. x The advantages of Starlink improve only over long distances (it reduces latency) & in remote areas. x Starlink cannot handle high load akin to a cell tower being overloaded with too many users. 'Project Loon', sometimes seen in the news, is related to (UPSC Prelims 2016) a) Waste management technology b) Wireless communication technology c) Solar power production technology d) Water conservation technology Voice over Wi-Fi (VoWiFi) x Bharti Airtel has introduced Voice over Wi-Fi (VoWiFi) which is a first for India. x VoWiFi calling makes use of high speed Internet to make and receive HD voice calls to any mobile or landline number across operators. x Wi-Fi calling can be configured on compatible smartphones that supports Wi-Fi calling. How does Voice over Wi-Fi benefit the mobile network operator (MNO)? PMF IAS – Learn Smart 59 x Employing VoWiFi enables MNOs to quickly and easily extend their coverage or service range without having to setup extra radio access network (RAN) infrastructure. x There is no need for new licensed spectrum or engaging in complex roaming agreements. How does VoWifi benefit the end user? x The end user will be able to make uninterrupted calls independent of the network’s cellular coverage. x Where possible, VoLTE calls can be seamlessly handed over between LTE and Wi-Fi and vice versa. x VoWif will improve voice calling in areas with weak cellular signals but stable WiFi connection. x It will particulary benefit rural areas, areas with tall structures where cellular network is poor, mountainous areas and indoors. How is VoWifi different from OTT calling? x VoWifi is not much different from a voice call using WhatsApp or any other over-the-top (OTT) messaging platform, but the call is from one number to another, and not using an app. How is VoWifi different from VoLTE? x In Voice over LTE (VoLTE), a MNO’s licensed spectrum (i.e. 4G LTE) is used to carry packetized voice. x In VoWifi, packetized voice is carried over high speed internet. x That is, in VoWifi calling cellular packets from the smartphone are transferred to the carrier over the internet and then injected back into the cellular network. Why are MNOs adopting VoWifi technology now? x VoWifi technology has been in place since a long time. x However, MNOs were hesitant to use VoWifi technology as that would hurt their voice-related revenue in- cluding revenue from roaming charges. x However, with the advent of VoLTE, MNO’s revenue base started shifting from voice & roaming charges to data charges. x Moreover, OTT applications like Whatsapp are eating out into MNO’s market share. x Hence, MNOs are taping into the VoWifi technology to regain the lost ground and stay relevant. Privacy and Data Protection Related Topics Data Localization and Data Protection PMF IAS – Learn Smart 60 What is Data Localization? x Data localisation is the act of storing data on any device physically present within the borders of a country. x Localisation mandates that companies collecting critical data about consumers must store & process them within the borders of the country. Why is it important? x The main intent behind data localisation is to protect the personal & financial information of the country’s citizens from foreign surveillance. x Storing of data locally is expected to help law–enforcement agencies to access information that is needed for the detection of a crime or to gather evidence. x On–shoring global data could also create domestic jobs & skills in data storage & analytics too. x Where data is not localised, the agencies need to rely on mutual legal assistance treaties (MLATs) to obtain access, delaying investigations. x Technologies like machine learning, Artificial Intelligence (AI) & Internet of Things (IoT) can produce tre- mendous value out of various data. It can be disastrous if data is not contained within boundaries. x To curtail the threatening of unregulated & arbitrary use of personal data, data localization is necessary. B.N Shrikrishna report on Data Protection x The SC in 2017 declared “privacy” a fundamental right. x A committee headed by retired SC Judge BN Srikrishna was constituted by GOI in 2017, to deliberate on a "Data Protection Framework". x The report has emphasized that interests of the citizens & the responsibilities of the state have to be pro- tected, but not at the cost of trade & industry. x The committee proposed a draft Personal Data Protection Bill. Highlights of the report and the proposed Personal Data Protection Bill PMF IAS – Learn Smart 61 Link: Source & Credits Individual Consent x The bill makes individual consent the centrepiece of data sharing, awards rights to users, imposes obliga- tions on data fiduciaries (person or organization that acts on behalf of another person, including the State). x It will make the data fiduciary liable for harms caused to the data principal. x It also calls for privacy by design on part of data processors, & defines terms like consent, data breach, etc. Right to be forgotten x It refers to the ability of individuals to limit, delink, delete, or correct the disclosure of personal information on the internet that is misleading, embarrassing, irrelevant, etc. Data Protection Authority x The law will set up a Data Protection Authority (DPA), which will be an independent regulatory body re- sponsible for the enforcement & effective implementation of the law. Personal Data x The law will cover processing of personal data by both public & private entities. x The law will have jurisdiction over the processing of personal data if such data has been used, shared, col- lected or otherwise processed in India. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 62 x It has proposed that critical personal data of Indians be processed in centres located within the country. x Additionally, personal data processed by companies incorporated under Indian law will be covered, irre- spective of where it is actually processed in India. Sensitive personal data x Sensitive personal data will include financial data, health data, sex life, sexual orientation, biometric & ge- netic data, caste, tribe, religious or political beliefs or affiliations of an individual. x DPA will be given the residuary power to notify further categories in accordance with the criteria set by law. Data Storage x The Bill makes it mandatory for a copy of personal data to be stored in India. Appellate Tribunal x The Central Government shall establish an appellate tribunal or grant powers to an existing appellate tribu- nal to hear & dispose of any appeal against an order of the DPA. Penalties x Penalties may be imposed for violations of the data protection law. x The penalties paid by violating entities will be deposited to a Data Protection Fund, which will, among other purposes, finance the functioning of the Data Protection Authority. Obligations on Fiduciaries x Obligations would include “purpose limitation” where data will be used only for clear, specific & lawful purposes & “collection limitation” where only data necessary for the purpose would be collected. Impact on allied laws x The report has also listed the impact of the proposed data protection framework on allied laws, including the Aadhaar Act & the RTI Act. x The committee has noted that the Aadhaar Act is silent on the powers of the Unique Identification Author- ity of India (UIDAI) to take enforcement action against errant companies in its ecosystem. x The report has also recommended amendments to the RTI Act, pointing out that disclosure of information from public authorities may lead to private harm being caused. Exceptions PMF IAS – Learn Smart 63 x The state can process data without consent of the user on ground of public welfare, law & order and emergency situations. x Processing of data for certain interests such as security of the State, legal proceedings, research & journal- istic purpose, may be exempt from certain obligations of the proposed data protection law. Cross border data transfers x Cross border data transfers of personal data will be through model contract clauses. x Personal data determined to be critical will be subject to the requirement to process only in India (there will be a prohibition against cross border transfer for such data). Data of Children x Committee has made specific mention of the need for separate & more stringent norms for protecting the data of children. Limitations x The Bill proposes that personal data of individuals can be processed for any function of the state. x This runs directly counter to the SC’s articulation of informed consent as central to informational privacy. x There is very little legislative & judicial oversight on surveillance activities and even the bill doesn’t include any safeguards concerning surveillance activities. GDPR vs Data Protection Bill x GDPR stands for General Data Protection Regulation that is in effect in EU since 2018. x It is a new set of rules designed to give EU citizens more control over their personal data. x GDPR framework applies to organisations in all EU member-states. x GDPR has almost become a common noun for personal data protection regulation. x Justice BN Srikrishna committee has referred to GDPR repeatedly. The key differences between GDPR and Data Protection Bill x GDPR is not an Act; individual member nations have enacted their own legislations based on GDPR. x Unlike in GDPR, Indian draft legislation does not require the data fiduciary to share the names and catego- ries of other recipients of the personal data with the data principal. x There is no obligation on data fiduciary to share with the data principal for how long the data will be stored while collecting or at any time, as GDPR mandates. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 64 x The data fiduciary does not need to share the source of the personal data to the data principal in case the data has not been collected from him/her which is an explicit requirement in GDPR x Unlike GDPR, there is no requirement that the data fiduciary share with the data principal the existence of automated decision making, including profiling. x In India, a citizen has not been given the right to demand his/her data to be erased. Data erasure, which is an article in itself in GDPR does not even find a mention in the Indian draft bill. x In case of a breach, there’s no requirement by Indian draft bill to share it with the data principal. This is also in contrast to GDPR provisions. x In India, every data fiduciary should ensure the storage of personal data locally. GDPR leaves this to spe- cific countries most of which have chosen to allow free flow of data. Virtual Private Network (VPN) x VPNs is a tool designed for large organisations to securely share their resources with their employees, as well as connect their employees and branches in a reduced-risk environment. x To ensure security, the VPN connection is established using an encrypted layered tunnelling protocol and users can use a host of authentication methods like passwords, certificates, to gain access to the network. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 65 x Since the line is encrypted between the network and the device connected to it, the traffic remains private. x VPN technology can check whether a connected device meets certain security requirements, thus making the connections secure. VPN and privacy x VPN is also a good tool to circumvent censorship. x We can connect securely to a proxy network via a VPN which, in turn, will connect to a destination website. x Whenever you are connected to the Internet, you are assigned an IP address – a numerical combination that is essentially similar to a regular street address. x With an IP address, you can be tracked down as easily as with a regular street address. x VPN replaces a user’s real IP addresses with the IP address of the gateway, which can be located in a different country. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 66 You may need a VPN it in the following cases x You do not want anyone to have access to the data you submit to the internet. x You do not want your ISP (Internet Service Provider) to know and log your internet activity. x You do not want various government agencies to track you and your actions on the internet. x You do not want various sites that you visit, and programs installed on your computer, to collect and send marketing information about you and about what you are doing on the internet. Kepler's laws of planetary motion (applicable to satellites also) x Kepler’s First Law: The orbit of a planet is an ellipse with the Sun at one of the two foci. x Kepler’s Second Law: A line segment joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas during equal intervals of time. x In simple words, the speed of the planet increases as it nears the sun and decreases as it recedes from the sun.
